criteria.commensurate: Homesteads, yes: the GM accepted +45% on that stage (prototype 9.85 to 14.38 s over nine seeds); measured here the reference total is +9.7% (17.81 to 19.54 s, medians of 3), and +11.3% in the bookend. Web at 40 households, no: +5.0 s summed over four seeds (+33% to +120% of the stage) is larger than the homesteads change at that size (-1.75 s), was never measured in the prototype the GM accepted, and buys nothing, since the ways laid are then pruned and last_resort drops none.
criteria.necessary: The gap pass, yes: FR-014/FR-015 and request.md Amendment 3 verbatim ('I still want A for how it shapes the map') replace the per-seat corridor search with it, and the counterfactual shows it is the homesteads growth (+0.37 to +0.67 s a reference map; the pass 0.69-0.94 s; the rest of the stage 0.21-0.45 s cheaper than main). The web's extra cost at 40 households is not necessary: prune_the_tree removing households' own laid ways one a round until the 8 rounds run out, then last_resort dropping nothing, is work the feature did not ask for, and the session's own later commit 25bdd8c3a forbids it ('pruned never').
criteria.no_way_around: There is a way around the web part: lay no way the web will prune, or never prune a household's laid way (25bdd8c3a does the latter, but at that HEAD the 40-household seed 4 roll is now WebRefused joins_short, so it must be re-measured on a new bookend). In the gap pass itself, flood() is a pure-Python heapq Dijkstra that indexes numpy cells one scalar at a time (research R4: about 0.4 s of the pass's 0.5-0.9 s), and lane_layers calls site_samples_clear once per uncertain cell; both are candidates, neither demonstrated here.
